result:
Consider that you have never actually seen light itself—only its traces. Light does not linger in places; it arrives, touches something, and leaves. The moon, for all its romantic reputation, produces nothing of its own. It is essentially a mirror wearing a coat of dust, returning borrowed sunlight to us at a slant. Even the sun we watch so reverently is merely the source, not the show. The show requires surfaces: grass, glass, skin, sea.

I find this quietly comforting. We live in a world of echoes made visible, and our entire picture of the cosmos rests on patience. When we look up, we see stars that may have died before the pyramids rose, galaxies whose present fate is already sealed but not yet delivered. Astronomy is largely the art of loving things as they used to be.

There is a human parallel hiding in this. No one meets you fully in real time. They meet your echo—the version of you that crossed the distance between two nervous systems, slightly delayed, refracted by whatever surfaces it touched along the way. An old friend sees you through light bounced off mirrors you polished years ago. Your mother still finds the child in your face because her attention lands on the oldest surfaces first.

Maybe that isn't a flaw in connection but its actual mechanism. We are each other's distant stars: perceived late, understood indirectly, revised constantly—and somehow, despite all the refraction, unmistakably bright.

Actually, let me write a lyrical piece about morning light moving through a house—it's relatable, visual, and can carry emotional depth. Or something more conceptual: the strange intimacy of reading words written by someone long dead.

Let me go with something about secondhand light—the idea that all light we've ever seen has bounced off things before reaching us, that we only ever perceive reflected light. That's scientifically true and philosophically rich. The sun's light bounces off the moon; everything we see is mediated. That could be beautiful.
